title.rendered: A Guide to Purchasing Disposable Suction Liner Bags for Healthcare Facilities

content.rendered:
Abstract

A disposable suction bag (also known as a disposable suction liner) is an important medical device used to collect secretions, blood, and other body fluids in hospitals and healthcare facilities. Selecting the right product can help reduce healthcare workers’ exposure to infectious fluids, prevent fluid overflow, protect the central suction system, and improve hospital waste management.

Suction bags differ in capacity, filter type, the presence or absence of gelling powder, and whether they are sterile or non-sterile. Procurement departments should therefore choose a product that is appropriate for the type of suction equipment, the expected volume of secretions, and the specific requirements of each department.

This article reviews the most important factors healthcare facilities should consider when purchasing disposable suction bags, as well as the features of the various Abadis disposable suction bag models.

What Is a Disposable Suction Bag?

During suctioning, secretions, blood, and other body fluids are conveyed through the suction tubing and collected in the suction bag. In older systems, these fluids were collected in fixed or reusable canisters, which had to be emptied, washed, and disinfected by support staff after each use.

In addition to consuming water, disinfectants, and staff time, this method increases the likelihood of direct contact with infectious secretions and waste.

A disposable suction bag is placed inside a reusable holder or outer canister, where it collects aspirated fluids. Once the bag is full, its ports are closed and the bag is disposed of in accordance with the healthcare facility’s waste-management procedures.

When used correctly, a disposable suction bag can provide the following benefits:

  • Reduced direct contact between staff and patients’ secretions
  • Support for infection-control practices in healthcare facilities
  • Less need to wash permanent canisters
  • Reduced consumption of water and disinfectants
  • Prevention of fluid ingress into the central suction system
  • Fast and easy bag replacement
  • More hygienic collection and disposal of secretions
  • Less time required to prepare the suction canister for reuse

Achieving these benefits, however, depends on selecting the appropriate product, installing it correctly, and following infection-control and waste-disposal procedures.

What Should You Consider When Purchasing Suction Bags?

Suction bags may look similar, but differences in capacity, filter type, connector quality, and the presence of gelling powder can affect how they perform in use.

The most important purchasing criteria for disposable suction bags are outlined below.

1. Selecting the Appropriate Capacity

Capacity is the first factor to consider when choosing a suction bag. Using a single capacity throughout an entire hospital is not always appropriate, because the volume of secretions varies from one department to another.

Using a small bag in high-use departments increases the frequency of bag changes. Conversely, using a large bag in low-use departments may occupy more space and increase the facility’s costs.

Abadis suction bags are manufactured in one-, two-, and three-liter capacities.

Bag capacity

 Suggested applications

1 liter

Ambulances, dentistry, ophthalmology, pediatrics, and other low-volume applications

2 liters

Pulmonology, endoscopy, gastroenterology, ICU, CCU, infectious disease wards, and inpatient wards
3 liters

Operating rooms, cardiovascular departments, procedures involving high fluid volumes, infectious disease wards, and liposuction

 

This classification is a general guide. The final choice should be based on the expected volume of secretions, the type of procedure, departmental consumption, and the assessment of the medical equipment or infection-control officer.

One-Liter Suction Bag

The one-liter suction bag is suitable for departments and applications in which relatively small volumes of secretions are typically collected. Its compact dimensions and lower capacity make it easier to use in ambulances, dental clinics, ophthalmology departments, and pediatric wards.

Before purchasing, the facility should confirm that the one-liter capacity is sufficient for the department’s needs and will not result in excessively frequent bag changes.

Two-Liter Suction Bag

The two-liter suction bag is a suitable option for general use in healthcare facilities. This capacity is used in departments such as pulmonology, endoscopy, gastroenterology, ICU, CCU, and inpatient wards.

The Abadis two-liter bag can be used on its own. When required, several bags may also be connected in series using the appropriate stand and connectors, increasing the total collection capacity to as much as 8 liters.

Three-Liter Suction Bag

The three-liter suction bag is suitable for departments and procedures in which larger volumes of fluid and secretions are collected. Operating rooms, cardiovascular departments, and certain surgical procedures are among the principal applications for this capacity.

With an appropriate stand and connectors, three-liter bags may also be connected in series to provide a total capacity of up to 12 liters. In procedures involving large volumes of fluid, this feature can reduce the need to replace a bag during surgery.

2. Considering the Suction Bag’s Filter Type

The filter is one of the most important components of a suction bag. Its primary function is to prevent fluid overflow and help protect the suction device or central suction system.

If collected fluid enters the vacuum line, it may contaminate the tubing, regulator, or central suction system. The type and performance of the filter should therefore be evaluated before purchase.

What Is a Hydrophobic Filter?

A hydrophobic filter is designed to prevent liquid from passing into the vacuum line. When the fluid level reaches the filter, the flow path is restricted or blocked, preventing the contents of the bag from overflowing into the suction system.

This feature is particularly useful in departments where substantial volumes of secretions are collected or where protecting the central suction system is especially important.

3. Presence of Gelling Powder

Some Abadis suction bags contain gelling powder. When the powder comes into contact with the collected fluids, it thickens or solidifies them into a gel.

Gelling the contents can reduce the free movement of liquid inside the bag and lower the risk of splashing or leakage during handling and disposal. The presence of gelling powder is therefore an important feature for improved management of hospital waste.

The benefits of gelling powder include:

  • Reduced movement of liquid inside the bag
  • Lower risk of splashing during transport
  • Easier handling of the filled bag
  • Support for more hygienic disposal of the contents
  • Lower risk of leakage during waste transfer

It is important to note that gelling powder does not disinfect the bag’s contents or render them non-infectious. A used bag must still be disposed of in accordance with the healthcare facility’s infectious-waste procedures.

Abadis suction bags are manufactured both with and without gelling powder. The procurement department should select the appropriate model based on the facility’s waste collection and disposal procedures.

4. Sterile or Non-Sterile Suction Bags

In many general hospital departments, the suction bag is positioned outside the sterile field, and a non-sterile model is sufficient.

In certain sensitive surgical procedures, however, or when fluids or tissue are to be sampled, a sterile model may be important.

The Abadis three-liter sterile suction bag is intended for procedures such as liposuction and other sensitive surgeries. It is supplied sterile and ready for use in the operating room, allowing safer sampling of collected fluids.

When purchasing a sterile suction bag, the following should be checked:

  • Packaging integrity
  • Confirmation that the package has not been opened or punctured
  • Manufacturing and expiration dates
  • Sterility information displayed on the product
  • Storage conditions
  • Exact product code
  • The manufacturer’s intended use

Sterility is a characteristic of a specific model and product code. It should therefore not be assumed that all suction bags produced by a particular brand are sterile.

5. Compatibility With Existing Suction Equipment and Canisters

Before purchase, the facility should confirm that the selected bag is compatible with its suction equipment, holder or outer canister, regulator, and existing connectors.

The bag must fit correctly inside the canister, and the lid must be secured without looseness or leakage. The patient port and vacuum port must also be compatible with the tubing used in the relevant department.

Abadis products are designed for use with central and portable suction systems. Nevertheless, before placing a bulk order, it is advisable to install and evaluate a product sample on the facility’s existing equipment.

When evaluating a sample, check the following:

  • The bag fits correctly inside the canister.
  • The lid is securely seated on the canister.
  • The vacuum tubing connects to the designated port.
  • The suction tubing connects to the patient port.
  • There are no air leaks.
  • The device provides adequate suction power.
  • The bag remains securely in place when suction begins.
  • The ports can be closed after use.

6. Quality of the Lid and Connectors

The quality of the lid and connectors is critical to the performance of a suction bag. If the lid does not fit the canister properly or the connection between the bag and the lid is weak, loss of suction or leakage is more likely.

A suitable suction bag should have the following characteristics:

  • A secure connection between the bag and the lid
  • Clearly identified patient and vacuum connection points
  • Effective sealing
  • Resistance to tearing
  • Ports that can be closed after use
  • Maintenance of suction power throughout use

7. Ability to Connect Multiple Bags in Series

In operating rooms and during certain surgical procedures, the capacity of a single bag may not be sufficient for the entire procedure. In such situations, connecting several bags in series can increase the total fluid-collection capacity.

In the Abadis system, two-liter bags can be connected in series using the appropriate stand and connectors to provide a total capacity of up to 8 liters. Three-liter bags can similarly be connected to provide a total capacity of up to 12 liters.

When purchasing bags for this purpose, ordering the bags alone is not sufficient. The procurement department must also consider the required stand, holders, and connectors.

Healthcare personnel must also be familiar with the correct method of connecting bags in series so that fluid enters the bags in the proper sequence and the system operates without loss of suction.

8. Ease of Installation and Use

Rapid equipment setup is important in hospitals. A bag that is difficult to install or has ports that are not clearly identified can increase the risk of user error.

A suitable suction bag should fit easily inside the canister, connect readily to the vacuum line, and be removable from the canister after use without direct contact with its contents.

Before placing a bulk order, it is advisable to provide several samples to the departments that will use the product. Nurses, operating-room personnel, and medical equipment staff can then evaluate how the bag is installed and used.

Proper user training is also essential. Even a high-quality product may lose suction, leak, or overflow if installed incorrectly.

9. Verification of Product Authorizations and Specifications

A suction bag is a consumable medical device and must carry verifiable specifications and regulatory authorizations. The procurement department should not check only the manufacturer’s name; it must verify the specifications of the exact model and product code being purchased.

Important information on the product and its packaging includes:

  • Manufacturer’s name
  • Product name and code
  • Bag capacity
  • Filter type
  • Presence or absence of gelling powder
  • Sterile or non-sterile status
  • IRC code or product registration identifier
  • Lot number
  • Manufacturing and expiration dates
  • Storage conditions
  • Number of units per carton

Recording the lot number when goods are received into inventory is important. If a problem arises or quality follow-up is required, the healthcare facility can identify the relevant shipment.

10. Price of Disposable Suction Bags

The price of a suction bag depends on several factors and should not be assessed solely on the basis of capacity.

The main factors affecting price include:

  • One-, two-, or three-liter capacity
  • Filter type
  • Presence of gelling powder
  • Sterile or non-sterile status
  • Order quantity
  • Type of packaging
  • Required accessories
  • Stands and holders
  • Connectors and tubing
  • Shipping and delivery terms

In institutional procurement, the lowest price does not always represent the best purchase. Lid quality, leak prevention, maintenance of suction power, filter performance, and ease of use should also be considered when comparing products.

Using disposable suction bags may also reduce some of the costs associated with washing fixed canisters, consuming water and disinfectants, and the time spent by support staff. The product’s price should therefore be evaluated alongside the ancillary costs of the facility’s current method.

How Can Each Department’s Required Capacity Be Determined?

To determine the required capacity and quantity, the procurement department can review each department’s consumption over a one-month period.

The following information should be collected:

  • Number of times suction is used in each department
  • Approximate volume of secretions
  • Number of bags used per day
  • Number of active beds
  • Number of surgical procedures
  • Potential for higher consumption on certain days
  • Lead time required for replenishment
  • Available storage space

Reviewing actual consumption helps prevent over-purchasing one capacity or running short of bags in high-use departments.

An appropriate level of safety stock should also be maintained for periods of increased consumption or supply delays, particularly in departments such as the ICU, emergency department, and operating room, where interruption of suction services is unacceptable.

Recommended Steps Before Placing a Bulk Order

To select the most appropriate suction bag, healthcare facilities are advised to take the following steps:

Identify Departmental Requirements

Prepare a list of the departments that use suction bags, the type of suction equipment in each department, the required capacity, and each department’s consumption level.

Select the Appropriate Model

Determine the required capacity, filter type, presence or absence of gelling powder, and sterile or non-sterile status based on the needs of each department.

Evaluate a Product Sample

Install a sample bag on the facility’s existing canisters and suction devices, and assess suction performance, absence of leakage, and ease of replacement.

Obtain Feedback From Healthcare Personnel

Nurses, operating-room staff, the medical equipment officer, and the infection-control officer should participate in evaluating the sample.

Record the Product Code

Once the sample has been approved, record the exact product code in the purchase request and contract to ensure that a different product is not delivered in place of the approved sample.

Provide Installation Training

Before distributing the product throughout the facility, train users in the correct procedures for installation, tubing connection, bag replacement, and disposal.

Common Mistakes When Purchasing Suction Bags

Certain purchasing mistakes can increase costs or cause problems during use:

  • Purchasing solely on the basis of the lowest price
  • Selecting a single capacity for all departments
  • Failing to consider the filter type
  • Purchasing a model without gelling powder for a department that requires a solidifying agent
  • Using a non-sterile model for an application that requires a sterile product
  • Failing to verify compatibility between the bag and the canister
  • Purchasing bags without the necessary stands and connectors
  • Failing to verify the IRC code and product specifications
  • Failing to record lot numbers in inventory records
  • Failing to train users in the correct installation procedure
  • Reusing a single-use bag
  • Disposing of the bag contrary to the hospital’s waste-management procedures

Disposable Suction Bag Purchasing Checklist

Before finalizing an order, answer the following questions:

  • Which department is the bag being purchased for?
  • What is the typical volume of secretions in that department?
  • Is a one-, two-, or three-liter capacity most appropriate?
  • Is the ability to connect multiple bags in series required?
  • What type of filter should be selected?
  • Does the product need to contain gelling powder?
  • Does the department require a sterile bag?
  • Is the bag compatible with the facility’s existing canister and suction equipment?
  • Are a stand, holder, or additional connectors required?
  • Has a product sample been tested on the facility’s equipment?
  • Are the product code and IRC code clearly specified?
  • Are the manufacturing and expiration dates acceptable?
  • What quantity is required each month?
  • When will the product be delivered?
  • Will users receive installation and operating instructions?

Why Is Selecting the Right Abadis Suction Bag Model Important?

Abadis disposable suction bags are manufactured in a range of capacities and models. Filter type, the presence of gelling powder, and sterility are not the same across all models and depend on the specific product code.

For this reason, a purchase request should not simply state “Abadis suction bag.” The capacity, filter type, presence or absence of gelling powder, and sterile or non-sterile status must be specified precisely.

The Abadis product range makes it possible to select a more appropriate capacity and model for low-use departments, general wards, and operating rooms.

For a more precise recommendation, the healthcare facility can provide Abadis Medical Canisters specialists with information such as the department type, existing equipment, monthly consumption, and intended application.

Conclusion

When purchasing disposable suction bags, several characteristics must be evaluated together. Bag capacity, filter type, the presence of gelling powder, sterile or non-sterile status, equipment compatibility, and the quality of the lid and connectors are among the most important selection criteria.

One-liter bags are more suitable for low-volume applications, two-liter bags for general departmental use, and three-liter bags for operating rooms and high-volume applications. When required, several bags can also be connected in series using the appropriate stand and connectors.

Choosing the right suction bag can support more hygienic collection of secretions, reduce healthcare workers’ direct contact with infectious fluids, protect the central suction system, and lower some of the costs associated with washing and disinfecting permanent canisters.

To select the appropriate capacity, filter type, and product code, contact the specialists at Abadis Medical Canisters. Before placing a bulk order, you can also test a product sample on the healthcare facility’s existing equipment.

Scientific References and Standards

  2. World Health Organization, “Safe management of wastes from health-care activities”
    Safe management of wastes from health-care activities
  3. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Best Practices for Single-Use Devices”
    Best Practices for Single-Use Devices – CDC
  4. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Reuse of Single-Use Medical Devices”
    Reuse of Single-Use Medical Devices – CDC
  5. U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, Occupational Exposure to Blood and Other Potentially Infectious Materials
    Bloodborne Pathogens Standard – OSHA
  6. International standard specifying general requirements for medical suction equipment
    ISO 10079-4:2021
  7. International standard specifying safety and performance requirements for suction equipment powered by a vacuum or positive-pressure gas source
    ISO 10079-3:2022
  8. StatPearls medical reference on the use and safe principles of airway secretion suctioning
    Surgical Airway Suctioning – NCBI Bookshelf
  9. Scientific article on surgical fluid and waste management and a comparison of collection systems
    Traditional canister-based open waste management system – PubMed

title.rendered: What Is an Oropharyngeal Airway (OPA)?

content.rendered:
What Is an Oropharyngeal Airway (OPA)? A Guide to Size Selection and Safe Use in Healthcare Facilities

Maintaining a patent airway is one of the first priorities when caring for critically ill, unconscious, or unresponsive patients. In these situations, reduced muscle tone in the jaw and tongue may cause the tongue to fall backward and obstruct airflow. If this obstruction is not relieved promptly, oxygen delivery may be compromised, increasing the risk of hypoxia, brain injury, and cardiac arrest.

One simple and practical device used to help maintain airway patency is the oropharyngeal airway. This device is also known as an OPA, oral airway, or Guedel airway. It is commonly used in emergency departments, operating rooms, intensive care units, ambulances, and resuscitation areas.

Despite its relatively simple design, selecting the wrong size or using an OPA in an unsuitable patient may worsen airway obstruction. Therefore, healthcare facilities should consider not only product quality but also size availability, the patient’s clinical condition, and the manufacturer’s instructions for use when purchasing and using these devices.

What Is an Oropharyngeal Airway?

An oropharyngeal airway is a curved medical device inserted through the mouth into the pharynx. It helps maintain an open airway by preventing the tongue from falling backward and obstructing airflow.

The device is typically manufactured from medical-grade polymeric materials and has a curvature designed to follow the anatomy of the mouth and pharynx. Its outer end has a flange that remains outside the mouth and helps prevent the device from being inserted too deeply.

An OPA is a temporary airway adjunct. It should not be confused with an endotracheal tube, laryngeal mask airway, or other advanced airway devices.

Main Components of an Oropharyngeal Airway

OPA design may vary by manufacturer, but most standard devices consist of the following components:

Flange

The flange remains outside the mouth and helps prevent the airway from moving too far into the pharynx. The device size or length is usually marked on or near this section.

Reinforced Bite Section or Bite Block

This section lies between the teeth and should be strong enough to resist deformation under normal biting pressure. However, an OPA should not be used solely as a bite block in every patient or clinical situation.

Curved Body

The curvature of the body is designed to follow the shape of the tongue and pharynx. When correctly positioned, it holds the tongue in a position that helps prevent airway obstruction.

Pharyngeal or Distal Tip

The distal end lies within the pharynx. Its length must be appropriate for the patient’s anatomy, as an airway that is too short or too long may not function properly and can cause complications.

Air Channel

The central or lateral channel allows air to pass through the device. Depending on the product design and clinical situation, some OPAs may also permit the passage of an appropriately sized suction catheter.

How Does an OPA Help Maintain Airway Patency?

In a conscious person, muscle activity in the jaw and tongue normally helps prevent upper airway obstruction. When the level of consciousness is significantly reduced, muscle tone decreases and the base of the tongue may move toward the posterior pharyngeal wall.

An OPA lies over the tongue and helps prevent it from falling backward and obstructing airflow. Correct placement may also make bag-mask ventilation easier and more effective.

According to the American Heart Association, the use of an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway may be reasonable in an unconscious or unresponsive patient without a cough or gag reflex to facilitate effective ventilation.

When Is an Oropharyngeal Airway Used?

Common indications for an OPA include:

  • Helping maintain airway patency in an unconscious patient without a gag reflex
  • Facilitating ventilation with a bag-valve mask
  • Supporting airway management during cardiopulmonary resuscitation by trained personnel
  • Providing temporary airway support in the operating room and during anesthesia
  • Assisting in the care of selected patients with a significantly reduced level of consciousness
  • Providing short-term airway support until a more advanced airway device is available
  • Facilitating access for suctioning secretions when permitted by the product design

An OPA should only be used after the patient has been appropriately assessed and by a trained healthcare professional. Unconsciousness alone is not sufficient; the presence or absence of cough and gag reflexes must also be evaluated.

When Should an OPA Not Be Used?

The most important contraindication to using an OPA is the presence of an active gag or cough reflex. Inserting an OPA in a conscious or semiconscious patient may cause gagging, vomiting, aspiration, or laryngospasm.

An OPA should generally not be used in the following situations:

  • The patient is conscious, responsive, or resisting
  • An active gag or cough reflex is present
  • There is severe trauma to the mouth, tongue, or pharynx
  • Mouth opening is severely restricted or trismus is present
  • A foreign body or fixed obstruction is present in the airway
  • The patient actively resists insertion
  • Insertion could worsen bleeding or tissue injury

If a patient begins coughing, gagging, vomiting, or resisting after OPA placement, tolerance of the device must be assessed immediately. Whether the device should remain in place or be removed must be determined according to the patient’s condition and the healthcare facility’s airway management protocol.

Does an OPA Prevent Secretions from Entering the Lungs?

No. An oropharyngeal airway is not a definitive airway and does not protect the lungs from blood, saliva, gastric contents, or other secretions.

It also cannot remove foreign bodies or fluids from the mouth and pharynx. If secretions, blood, or vomit are present, appropriate airway clearance and suctioning remain necessary.

An OPA must not be considered a substitute for endotracheal intubation, suctioning, oxygen therapy, or any other intervention required by the patient.

What Is the Difference Between an OPA and an Endotracheal Tube?

An OPA is positioned only within the mouth and pharynx. It does not pass through the larynx or enter the trachea. Its main purpose is to help prevent the tongue from obstructing the airway.

An endotracheal tube passes through the vocal cords and into the trachea. It is used for mechanical ventilation, controlled oxygen delivery, and advanced airway management.

Therefore, an OPA is a temporary airway adjunct, whereas an endotracheal tube can provide an advanced and relatively protected airway when correctly placed in an appropriate patient.

What Is the Difference Between an Oropharyngeal and a Nasopharyngeal Airway?

An oropharyngeal airway, or OPA, is inserted through the mouth and is generally suitable for an unconscious patient without a gag reflex.

A nasopharyngeal airway, or NPA, is inserted through the nose and may be better tolerated by some patients who retain a degree of consciousness or an intact gag reflex. However, NPAs have their own limitations and contraindications. For example, they should not be used without specialist assessment in certain cases of severe facial trauma or suspected basilar skull fracture.

The choice between an OPA and an NPA should be based on the patient’s condition, the nature of any injury, and the applicable airway management protocol.

Why Is Correct OPA Size Selection Important?

Selecting the correct size is one of the most important factors affecting OPA safety and effectiveness. The appropriate size cannot be determined solely by the patient’s age or sex or by the device color because facial and mandibular anatomy varies between individuals.

OPA Too Short

If the OPA is shorter than required, it may fail to hold the tongue in the correct position. In some cases, an airway that is too short may push the tongue backward and worsen airway obstruction.

OPA Too Long

An excessively long OPA may be inserted too deeply and apply pressure to the epiglottis, larynx, or surrounding soft tissues. This may cause tissue injury, coughing, gagging, laryngospasm, or airway obstruction.

How to Select the Correct OPA Size

One commonly used method of estimating the appropriate size is to hold the OPA alongside the patient’s face. In this method:

  • The flange is positioned beside the lips or at the corner of the mouth.
  • The distal tip should approximately reach the angle of the mandible.

Some clinical references use the distance from the maxillary incisors to the angle of the mandible as an alternative external measurement. Clinical studies suggest that external facial measurements can help with initial size selection, but the final assessment should be based on the individual patient’s anatomy and clinical condition.

Color coding may make size selection faster. However, colors and numbering systems may vary among manufacturers. Healthcare personnel should therefore verify the nominal length and size marking in addition to the device color.

OPA Sizing for Pediatric and Adult Patients

OPAs are generally available in neonatal, pediatric, and adult sizes. Common product ranges may include lengths of approximately 40 to 110 millimeters, although the exact size range and numbering system must be confirmed using the manufacturer’s documentation.

Using a fixed age-based table without an anatomical measurement is not an appropriate method of selecting an OPA. Healthcare facilities should maintain a range of sizes suitable for the patient populations they serve.

For example, some resuscitation equipment lists recommend sizes 2, 3, and 4 for adult patients. However, this should not be treated as a universal rule for every patient. Pediatric, neonatal, and emergency departments require a broader range of sizes appropriate to their patient population.

Additional caution is required when considering an OPA for premature infants. Resuscitation Council UK guidance warns that an OPA may contribute to airway obstruction in some infants born before 34 weeks of gestation.

General Principles of OPA Insertion

OPA insertion is a clinical procedure and should only be performed by trained personnel in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions and the healthcare facility’s airway management protocol.

Before insertion, the mouth and airway should be assessed and, when necessary, cleared of visible secretions, blood, or foreign material. The correct size should then be selected, and the device should be inserted without excessive force.

In adults, either a controlled rotation technique or direct insertion with the assistance of a tongue depressor may be used. In children, direct insertion while controlling the tongue is generally preferred because rotating the device may injure the hard or soft palate or push the tongue backward.

After placement, the following should be assessed:

  • Airway patency
  • Adequate chest movement
  • Quality of bag-mask ventilation
  • Abnormal airway sounds
  • Oxygen saturation and respiratory status
  • Coughing, gagging, or patient resistance
  • Correct position of the flange outside the mouth

The presence of an OPA in the mouth does not guarantee a patent airway. The patient must be monitored continuously.

Potential Complications of Incorrect OPA Use

Inappropriate use, incorrect size selection, or placement in a patient with an intact gag reflex may cause the following complications:

  • Gagging, nausea, and vomiting
  • Aspiration of gastric contents
  • Laryngospasm
  • Injury to the tongue, palate, lips, or pharynx
  • Mucosal bleeding
  • Dental injury
  • Excessive pressure on oral tissues
  • Worsening airway obstruction
  • Device displacement or expulsion
  • Delay in establishing a required advanced airway

To reduce these risks, healthcare personnel must be trained in OPA size selection, insertion, and patient monitoring.

A Purchasing Guide for Healthcare Facilities

Procurement managers and medical equipment personnel should not select an OPA based solely on price or color coding. The design and manufacturing quality of this device are directly related to patient airway safety.

Compliance With Applicable Standards

ISO 5364:2026 specifies requirements for oropharyngeal airways. ISO 18190:2025 sets out general requirements for airway devices and related equipment, including requirements concerning design, materials, marking, packaging, and information supplied by the manufacturer.

Before purchasing, the product’s technical documentation and compliance with the standards and regulatory requirements of the destination market should be reviewed.

Complete Range of Sizes

The available size range should correspond to the patient population served by the healthcare facility. General hospitals, emergency departments, and facilities with pediatric units require a wider range of sizes than adult-only centers.

Clearly Marked Size and Length

The airway size or length should be clearly and legibly marked on the device or flange. Color coding can accelerate identification, but it should not be the only method used to determine device size.

Surface and Edge Quality

The OPA surface should be smooth and free from sharp edges, burrs, or other features that could injure the patient. The distal tip and flange should also be appropriately designed to reduce the risk of mucosal trauma.

Strength of the Bite Section

The section positioned between the teeth should have sufficient strength to resist deformation or breakage under normal clinical pressure.

Appropriate Air-Channel Design

The internal channel should be open and uniform. Deformation, obstruction, or an abnormal reduction in cross-sectional area may increase resistance to airflow.

Packaging Quality

Packaging should protect the product against contamination, physical damage, and deformation. For sterile products, the integrity of the sterile barrier, sterilization method, and expiration date should be verified.

Traceability

A lot or batch number, manufacturing date, expiration date where applicable, manufacturer’s name, product specifications, and valid registration information help ensure effective product control and traceability.

Single-Use or Reusable Designation

If an OPA is labeled for single use, it must not be reused or reprocessed. Reusing a single-use device may compromise its performance, strength, cleanliness, and safety.

Sample Evaluation Before Bulk Purchasing

Before placing a bulk order, a sample should ideally be evaluated by the medical equipment department, an anesthesiologist, the emergency team, or the resuscitation officer. Important evaluation criteria include the clarity of size markings, surface quality, structural strength, ease of opening the packaging, and compatibility with the facility’s clinical workflow.

Oropharyngeal Airway Purchasing Checklist

Before finalizing a purchase, review the following:

  • A size range appropriate for the patient population
  • Clear size numbering and length markings
  • Recognizable and documented color coding
  • Smooth surfaces without potentially harmful edges
  • Adequate strength of the bite section
  • An open, undeformed air channel
  • Intact and durable packaging
  • Clearly stated sterile or non-sterile status
  • Clearly stated single-use or reusable designation
  • Clear instructions for use, including a Persian version where required for the Iranian market
  • Lot or batch identification and product traceability
  • Manufacturing and expiration dates where applicable
  • Valid technical documentation and regulatory approvals
  • Appropriate storage and transportation requirements
  • Reliable availability of frequently used sizes

Conclusion

An oropharyngeal airway is a simple but important device for temporary airway management. In an unconscious patient without a gag reflex, it can help prevent the tongue from obstructing the airway and may facilitate bag-mask ventilation.

The safety and effectiveness of an OPA depend on three main factors: appropriate patient selection, correct size selection, and proper placement by a trained professional. An incorrectly sized OPA or its use in a patient with an intact gag reflex may cause tissue injury, vomiting, aspiration, or worsening airway obstruction instead of improving the patient’s condition.

When purchasing OPAs, healthcare facilities should consider manufacturing standards, size range, surface quality, structural strength, marking, packaging, and product traceability. For information about available sizes, technical specifications, and supply conditions, please contact the specialists at Makhazen Tebi Abadis.

This article is intended to provide a scientific introduction to oropharyngeal airways. It is not a substitute for hands-on clinical training, the manufacturer’s instructions for use, or the healthcare facility’s airway management protocol.

title.rendered: What Is a Nelaton Catheter?

content.rendered:
Introduction

Safe and effective bladder drainage is an important aspect of care for many hospitalized and outpatient patients. Urinary catheters may become essential in conditions such as urinary retention, certain neurological disorders, spinal cord injuries, urological procedures, or situations in which a patient is unable to empty the bladder naturally.

Among the different types of urinary catheters, the Nelaton catheter is one of the most widely used single-use catheters in healthcare facilities because of its simple design, suitable flexibility, and broad range of applications. It is designed for temporary bladder drainage and, unlike a Foley catheter, has no retention balloon. It is therefore removed after the bladder has been emptied and is not intended for indwelling or long-term use.

Nelaton catheters are widely used in hospitals, operating rooms, emergency departments, rehabilitation centers, specialist clinics, and by certain patients who require intermittent catheterization. Selecting the correct size, following appropriate aseptic practices, and using a high-quality product are important for reducing the risk of urinary tract infection, urethral injury, and other complications.

This article explains the structure, applications, types, sizes, standard color coding, potential complications, and relevant manufacturing standards of Nelaton catheters. It also discusses the differences between Nelaton catheters and other urinary catheters and outlines important considerations for their selection and use.

What Is a Nelaton Catheter?

A Nelaton catheter is a sterile, flexible, single-use, non-balloon urinary catheter used for temporary drainage of urine from the bladder or for collecting a sterile urine specimen. It is inserted through the urethra into the bladder and removed once the bladder has been emptied.

The catheter is named after Auguste Nélaton, a prominent nineteenth-century French surgeon who contributed to the development of surgical and medical instruments.

Unlike a Foley catheter, which contains a balloon and is designed to remain in the bladder, a Nelaton catheter has no retention mechanism. It is therefore primarily used when temporary or intermittent bladder drainage is required.

Nelaton catheters are commonly made of medical-grade PVC, although some models are manufactured from polyurethane or silicone. These materials provide suitable flexibility and adequate mechanical strength, allowing the catheter to pass through the urethra while minimizing tissue trauma.

A Nelaton catheter typically has one or two side eyes near its distal end through which urine enters the catheter. Its smooth, rounded tip is designed to minimize the risk of injury to the urethral mucosa.

Main Components of a Nelaton Catheter

Although a Nelaton catheter has a relatively simple structure, each component is designed to support safe and effective use.

Catheter Shaft

The catheter shaft is a flexible, hollow tube that allows urine to flow from the bladder to the outside of the body. Its external diameter is specified using the French scale (Fr or Ch), and Nelaton catheters are manufactured in a range of sizes.

Rounded Tip

The distal tip of a Nelaton catheter is smooth and rounded to reduce friction and minimize trauma during passage through the urethra.

Side Eyes

One or two side openings are positioned near the catheter tip to allow urine to enter the lumen. Properly finished side eyes help support smooth and effective bladder drainage.

Proximal Connector

The proximal end of the catheter is fitted with a color-coded connector. In addition to facilitating connection to compatible equipment, the connector color helps identify the catheter size according to the applicable international color-coding system.

Features of a Nelaton Catheter

The simple and practical design of the Nelaton catheter provides several important features:

  • Sterile and ready for use
  • Intended for single use
  • No retention balloon
  • Suitable flexibility to reduce urethral trauma
  • Smooth surface for easier passage
  • Rounded, atraumatic tip
  • Available in different sizes for neonates, children, and adults
  • Color-coded connector corresponding to the French size
  • Suitable for temporary bladder drainage and sterile urine specimen collection

How Does a Nelaton Catheter Work?

A Nelaton catheter works by creating a temporary pathway through which urine can drain from the bladder.

After the catheter is passed through the urethra and its tip reaches the bladder, urine enters the catheter through the side eyes. It then flows through the lumen and exits through the proximal end as a result of the pressure difference and gravity.

Because the Nelaton catheter has no balloon, it is gently removed by a healthcare professional—or by an appropriately trained patient during intermittent self-catheterization—after bladder drainage is complete.

As it does not remain in the bladder, it avoids complications specifically associated with prolonged indwelling catheterization, such as encrustation, catheter blockage, and the increased infection risk associated with extended catheter dwell time.

The Nelaton catheter is therefore suitable for intermittent catheterization and a range of short-term diagnostic and therapeutic procedures.

Applications of the Nelaton Catheter

The Nelaton catheter is one of the most commonly used urinary catheters in healthcare facilities and may be used for various diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Its simple design, suitable flexibility, and short-term use make it an appropriate option for temporary bladder drainage and certain medical procedures.

The decision to use a Nelaton catheter should be based on the patient’s clinical condition, the expected duration of catheterization, the intended purpose, and the clinician’s judgment.

Its main applications include the following:

1. Temporary Bladder Drainage

The primary application of a Nelaton catheter is temporary drainage of urine from the bladder.

Some patients are unable to empty their bladder naturally. Accumulated urine can cause pain, bladder distension, kidney injury, and an increased risk of infection. In appropriate clinical circumstances, a Nelaton catheter creates a temporary drainage pathway and allows the bladder to be emptied.

Urinary retention may be associated with conditions such as:

  • Acute urinary retention
  • Chronic urinary retention
  • Prostatic enlargement
  • Urethral narrowing or obstruction
  • Neurogenic bladder dysfunction
  • Adverse effects of certain medications
  • Postoperative urinary retention

Because a Nelaton catheter is removed after drainage, it does not expose the patient to the risks associated with leaving a catheter in the bladder for an extended period.

2. Collection of a Sterile Urine Specimen

Another important application of the Nelaton catheter is the collection of a urine specimen for diagnostic testing when catheterized sampling is clinically indicated.

A naturally voided urine specimen may sometimes be contaminated by bacteria from the skin or genital area, potentially affecting test results. Catheterized urine collection can provide a specimen with a lower risk of external contamination when performed correctly and may be appropriate when more controlled sampling is required.

3. Use in the Operating Room

Nelaton catheters may also be used during certain surgical procedures.

For some short procedures, emptying the bladder before surgery may improve surgical access and help reduce the risk of inadvertent bladder injury. A Nelaton catheter may also be used after certain procedures to confirm that the bladder has been emptied.

4. Use in the Emergency Department

Rapid clinical assessment is essential in emergency care. Following appropriate evaluation, a Nelaton catheter may be used for temporary bladder drainage in situations such as acute urinary retention, reduced consciousness, or certain acute medical conditions.

Prompt bladder drainage may improve patient comfort and assist with clinical assessment. In trauma cases, however, possible urethral injury must be considered before urethral catheterization is attempted.

5. Use in Patients With Neurological Disorders

Patients with spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, spina bifida, or other neurological conditions may lose the ability to empty their bladder completely.

For many of these patients, clinicians may recommend clean intermittent catheterization (CIC). In this method, the patient or a trained caregiver inserts a suitable intermittent catheter at scheduled intervals to empty the bladder and then removes it.

When clinically appropriate and correctly performed, intermittent catheterization may reduce the risk of certain complications compared with continuous use of an indwelling catheter.

6. Use in Intensive Care Units

Some patients in intensive care, particularly those with reduced consciousness or limited mobility, may occasionally require temporary bladder drainage.

The clinician must determine whether intermittent drainage with a Nelaton catheter is appropriate or whether an indwelling catheter, such as a Foley catheter, is necessary for the patient’s condition.

7. Use in Children and Neonates

Nelaton catheters are manufactured in small sizes suitable for children and neonates.

In pediatric units, neonatal intensive care units, and pediatric intensive care units, these catheters may be used for:

  • Temporary bladder drainage
  • Catheterized urine specimen collection
  • Assessment of urinary tract function
  • Certain diagnostic and therapeutic procedures

Because pediatric urinary tissues are particularly delicate, selecting the correct catheter size and following proper catheterization technique are especially important.

8. Use in Female and Male Patients

Nelaton catheters may be used in both female and male patients.

However, the male urethra is longer than the female urethra. This anatomical difference must be considered when selecting the appropriate catheter length and performing catheterization.

Benefits of Nelaton Catheters for Short-Term Use

When only temporary bladder drainage is required, a Nelaton catheter may offer several advantages:

  • Rapid and effective bladder drainage
  • No need for the catheter to remain in the body
  • Reduced post-procedure discomfort after removal
  • Suitable for intermittent catheterization
  • Can be used for catheterized urine specimen collection
  • Straightforward use by trained healthcare personnel
  • Available in different sizes for various age groups

Types of Nelaton Catheters

Although the general design of Nelaton catheters is similar across models, they are available in different sizes, lengths, materials, and age-specific configurations to meet the needs of different patients and healthcare settings.

The appropriate type should be selected according to the patient’s age, sex, clinical condition, intended use, and the clinician’s judgment.

The main classifications are as follows:

1. Nelaton Catheters by French Size

The most common method of classifying Nelaton catheters is the French scale (Fr or Ch). This scale indicates the catheter’s external diameter: the higher the French number, the larger the catheter diameter.

Correct size selection is important. A catheter that is unnecessarily large may increase discomfort and the risk of urethral trauma, while a catheter that is too small may result in slow or ineffective drainage.

Common Nelaton Catheter Sizes

Size (Fr) Standard Connector Color Common Application
6 Fr Light green Neonates and infants
8 Fr Blue Children
10 Fr Black Older children and adolescents
12 Fr White Smaller adults
14 Fr Green One of the commonly used adult sizes
16 Fr Orange Adults
18 Fr Red Situations requiring a larger drainage lumen
20 Fr Yellow Selected clinical indications under medical supervision
22 Fr Violet Limited or specialist applications
24 Fr Dark blue Selected urological applications

Note: Connector color coding should be verified against the applicable standard and the manufacturer’s documentation. Minor differences may exist between products or markets.

2. Nelaton Catheters by Age Group

Nelaton catheters are manufactured for different age groups.

Neonatal Nelaton Catheters

These catheters have a very small diameter and a soft shaft suitable for neonatal and infant use.

Pediatric Nelaton Catheters

Smaller-diameter catheters are used in pediatric, NICU, and PICU settings to reduce the risk of urethral trauma.

Adult Nelaton Catheters

Commonly used adult sizes are often within the 12 to 16 Fr range, although the final selection must be based on the patient’s anatomy, clinical condition, and the clinician’s judgment.

3. Nelaton Catheters by Material

Nelaton catheters may be manufactured from different materials, each with specific characteristics.

Medical-Grade PVC

Medical-grade PVC is commonly used to manufacture Nelaton catheters.

Its potential characteristics include:

  • Suitable flexibility
  • Adequate mechanical strength
  • Cost-effective manufacturing
  • Smooth surface
  • Suitability for single-use products

Silicone

Some specialized models are made of silicone, which may provide greater flexibility and biocompatibility. These products may also be more expensive to manufacture.

Polyurethane

Polyurethane may be used for certain specialized products because it can provide an appropriate combination of mechanical strength and flexibility.

4. Nelaton Catheters by Length

Catheter length varies according to the intended patient group and application.

In general:

  • Pediatric catheters are shorter.
  • Adult catheters are longer.
  • Some models are specifically designed for male or female anatomy.

How Is the Appropriate Nelaton Catheter Size Selected?

The appropriate catheter size should be selected by a clinician or trained healthcare professional according to the patient’s clinical condition.

Relevant factors include:

  • Patient age
  • Sex
  • Urethral anatomy
  • Purpose of catheterization
  • Presence of urethral narrowing, obstruction, or injury
  • Underlying medical conditions
  • Overall clinical status

In general, the smallest catheter size that provides effective drainage should be selected. This approach may reduce urethral trauma and patient discomfort.

Difference Between a Nelaton Catheter and a Foley Catheter

Nelaton and Foley catheters are both widely used urinary catheters, but they differ significantly in design, duration of use, and clinical application.

The choice between them depends on factors such as the patient’s condition, the required duration of bladder drainage, the underlying disorder, and the clinician’s judgment.

Nelaton Catheter

A Nelaton catheter is a sterile, single-use, non-balloon catheter designed for temporary bladder drainage. After the catheter enters the bladder and drainage is complete, it is removed. It is not intended to remain in the bladder or be reused.

Nelaton catheters are commonly used for intermittent catheterization, catheterized urine specimen collection, diagnostic procedures, and certain short-duration surgical applications.

Foley Catheter

A Foley catheter is an indwelling urinary catheter with a retention balloon near its distal end. After the catheter enters the bladder, the balloon is inflated with the volume and fluid specified by the manufacturer to retain the catheter in position.

Foley catheters are used when continuous bladder drainage is clinically required, such as in selected intensive care patients, during or after certain surgical procedures, or in patients with severe urinary dysfunction.

Comparison of Nelaton and Foley Catheters

Feature Nelaton Catheter Foley Catheter
Duration of use Temporary and short-term Short-term or longer-term, as clinically indicated
Retention balloon No Yes
Remains in the bladder No Yes
Primary application Temporary bladder drainage and catheterized urine sampling Continuous bladder drainage
Common settings Emergency care, operating rooms, clinics, and intermittent catheterization Intensive care, inpatient care, perioperative care, and other indications requiring continuous drainage
Infection risk Generally lower when used correctly and removed promptly Increases with prolonged indwelling use
Patient considerations Suitable when only temporary drainage is required Suitable when continuous drainage is clinically necessary
Reusable No No; duration of use must follow clinical guidance and the manufacturer’s instructions

When Is a Nelaton Catheter Used?

Clinicians may select a Nelaton catheter in situations such as:

  • Temporary bladder drainage
  • Acute urinary retention, following appropriate assessment
  • Catheterized urine specimen collection
  • Intermittent catheterization
  • Certain diagnostic or therapeutic procedures
  • Selected short-duration surgical procedures

The absence of a balloon allows the catheter to be removed after the procedure, eliminating the need for it to remain in the bladder.

When Is a Foley Catheter More Appropriate?

A Foley catheter may be selected when continuous urine drainage is clinically required, including in circumstances such as:

  • Selected cases of prolonged hospitalization
  • Intensive care
  • Certain major surgical procedures
  • Accurate monitoring of urine output in appropriately selected patients
  • Certain severe bladder-emptying disorders

In these situations, the retention balloon helps prevent unintentional catheter displacement and enables continuous urine drainage.

Can a Nelaton Catheter Replace a Foley Catheter?

No. Nelaton and Foley catheters are designed for different clinical purposes, and the choice between them must be based on the patient’s condition and the clinician’s judgment.

Using a Nelaton catheter when continuous drainage is required, or using an indwelling Foley catheter when temporary drainage is sufficient, may be inappropriate.

Each catheter therefore has a defined role in patient care. Correct selection can help improve patient safety, reduce complications, and support better clinical outcomes.

Advantages of the Nelaton Catheter

Because of its simple design, ease of use, and suitability for short-term bladder drainage, the Nelaton catheter is widely used in hospitals and other healthcare settings.

Its principal advantages include the following:

1. Suitable for Temporary Bladder Drainage

One of the main advantages of the Nelaton catheter is that it is designed for short-term catheterization. After the bladder has been emptied, the catheter is removed and does not need to remain in place.

This can improve patient comfort after the procedure and avoids the restrictions associated with an indwelling urinary catheter.

2. Potentially Lower Infection Risk Than Indwelling Catheters

Any foreign object that remains in the body can create conditions that support microbial colonization. Because a Nelaton catheter remains in the bladder only briefly, correctly performed intermittent catheterization may carry a lower infection risk than prolonged indwelling catheterization.

However, no urinary catheter is completely risk-free. Hand hygiene, appropriate catheterization technique, suitable equipment, and adherence to infection-prevention procedures remain essential.

3. Simple Design and Straightforward Use

The Nelaton catheter has a simple structure and contains no balloon, inflation valve, or other mechanical retention components. This makes it relatively straightforward for trained healthcare professionals to use.

Patients who have received appropriate assessment and training may also use a suitable catheter for clean intermittent self-catheterization.

4. Design Intended to Reduce Urethral Trauma

The rounded tip and smooth catheter surface are designed to minimize friction against the urethral wall. When the correct size and technique are used, these features may reduce mucosal trauma, pain, and bleeding.

5. Available in a Wide Range of Sizes

Nelaton catheters are produced in various sizes suitable for different age groups, from neonates to adults.

This range allows clinicians to choose a catheter appropriate for the patient’s anatomy and clinical needs.

6. Suitable for Catheterized Urine Specimen Collection

In certain clinical situations, a urine specimen with minimal external contamination may be required. When clinically indicated and performed correctly, a Nelaton catheter can be used to collect a catheterized specimen and may improve the reliability of certain diagnostic tests.

7. Cost-Effective Design

Because of its simple construction and single-use design, the Nelaton catheter may be a cost-effective option for many healthcare facilities.

Nevertheless, product quality, manufacturing standards, sterility, and safety should take priority over price alone.

Limitations of the Nelaton Catheter

Despite its advantages, a Nelaton catheter is not suitable for every patient or clinical situation.

1. Not Intended for Indwelling Use

The main limitation of a Nelaton catheter is the absence of a retention balloon. It must be removed after bladder drainage and is unsuitable for patients who require continuous urine drainage.

In these circumstances, the clinician may consider an indwelling catheter such as a Foley catheter.

2. Need for Repeated Catheterization

Patients who cannot empty their bladder naturally may need intermittent catheterization at scheduled intervals.

This requires appropriate training, careful hygiene, and cooperation from the patient or caregiver.

3. Risk of Injury if Used Incorrectly

Using an inappropriate size, applying excessive force, or performing catheterization incorrectly can cause urethral injury, bleeding, or the creation of a false passage.

Catheterization should therefore be performed by trained personnel or by patients and caregivers who have received appropriate clinical instruction.

4. Risk of Infection if Proper Technique Is Not Followed

Although intermittent catheterization may reduce some risks associated with indwelling catheters, poor hand hygiene, inappropriate technique, use of a nonsterile or compromised product, or contamination of the catheter may increase the risk of urinary tract infection.

Correct Selection Is More Important Than Catheter Type Alone

No single urinary catheter is the best option for every patient. The choice between a Nelaton catheter, Foley catheter, or another urinary catheter must be based on the patient’s clinical condition, the required duration of catheterization, infection risk, and the clinician’s judgment.

In addition to product quality, correct size selection, proper catheterization technique, and appropriate infection-prevention measures play important roles in achieving successful drainage and reducing complications.

Important Considerations When Selecting and Using a Nelaton Catheter

Correct selection and use of a Nelaton catheter are important for reducing complications and improving patient safety.

Factors such as catheter size, sterility, material quality, product integrity, intended use, and compliance with applicable manufacturing requirements should be considered.

Appropriate catheterization technique, suitable lubrication when required, and performance of the procedure by trained individuals can help reduce urethral trauma and urinary tract infection.

Because the Nelaton catheter is a single-use medical device, it must be discarded after use in accordance with the healthcare facility’s medical-waste procedures. It must not be reused.

Potential Complications of Nelaton Catheter Use

When used correctly, a Nelaton catheter can provide safe and effective temporary bladder drainage. Nevertheless, incorrect use may be associated with complications such as:

  • Urinary tract infection
  • Irritation or injury of the urethral mucosa
  • Pain or discomfort during catheterization
  • Minor bleeding caused by mucosal trauma
  • Bladder spasm in some patients
  • Creation of a false passage in the event of traumatic insertion

Appropriate infection-prevention measures, selection of the correct size, suitable lubrication, gentle technique, and use of an intact sterile catheter are important for reducing these risks.

Important Standards for Nelaton Catheter Manufacturing

As a medical device, a Nelaton catheter should be manufactured in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements and recognized standards.

Relevant standards and regulations may include:

  • ISO 13485:2016 — Medical devices — Quality management systems — Requirements for regulatory purposes
  • ISO 20696:2018 — Sterile urethral catheters for single use
  • Regulation (EU) 2017/745 — European Union Medical Device Regulation
  • ISO 10993 series — Biological evaluation of medical devices

Compliance with applicable standards and regulatory requirements supports appropriate control of product design, manufacturing, quality, sterility, biocompatibility, and traceability.

Conclusion

The Nelaton catheter is a widely used urinary catheter designed primarily for temporary bladder drainage and catheterized urine specimen collection. Its simple structure, suitable flexibility, ease of use, and availability in multiple sizes have made it useful in hospitals, clinics, operating rooms, emergency departments, rehabilitation settings, and selected intensive care applications.

Safe and effective use depends on correct size selection, appropriate patient assessment, proper infection-prevention practices, use of a high-quality sterile product, and adherence to clinical guidance.

The catheter type should always be selected according to the patient’s clinical condition and the clinician’s judgment to achieve appropriate drainage while minimizing avoidable complications.

References

  1. World Health Organization (WHO). Medical Devices Technical Series.
  2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTI).
  3. European Association of Urology (EAU). EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections.
  4. American Urological Association (AUA). Clinical Guidance on Urinary Catheterization.
  5. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Healthcare-Associated Infections: Prevention and Control.
  6. National Health Service (NHS). Urinary Catheterisation Clinical Guidelines.
  7. ISO 13485:2016. Medical Devices — Quality Management Systems — Requirements for Regulatory Purposes.
  8. ISO 20696:2018. Sterile Urethral Catheters for Single Use.
  9. ISO 10993 Series. Biological Evaluation of Medical Devices.
  10. Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on Medical Devices.
